slides.title: The Rules Governing Adverse Action Notices
slides.description:
There are two rules that govern the issuing of adverse action notices:

  • FCRA – Fair Credit Reporting Act
  • ECOA – Equal Credit Opportunity Act

slides.title: ADVERSE ACTION NOTICES
slides.description:
• Both the Fair Credit Reporting Act FCRA, and Equal Credit Opportunity Act ECOA require a creditor to provide a consumer an “Adverse Action Notice” when credit is denied.
  • Adverse action is defined as a refusal to grant credit in substantially the amount, or on substantially the terms, requested on an application, unless a counteroffer is made and accepted by the applicant.

slides.title: WHO MUST PROVIDE AN ADVERSE ACTION NOTICE?
slides.description: • A Creditor, in this case an automobile dealership, must provide an adverse action notice to a consumer when credit is denied, not even submitted for approval, or not granted upon the terms requested, and the decision is based on whole or in part on information contained in a consumer report.

slides.title: WHO IS A CREDITOR?
slides.description:
• The dealer cannot find a lending institution willing to accept the application for credit
  • No lending institution is willing to accept the terms of the retail installment contract created from a spot delivery
  • Customer rejects the counter offer as a result of a change in terms acceptable to the lending institution

slides.title: ECOA NOTICE
slides.description:
• The ECOA and Reg. B require a creditor to provide an adverse action notice when an adverse decision is made in a consumer credit transaction.
  • An Adverse Action Notice required under the ECOA must be sent to a consumer regardless of whether they fall within one of the protected classes under the act. Simply put, the notice required under the ECOA must be given to all consumers denied financing, or not granted financing upon terms requested, and no counter offer is accepted.

slides.title: FCRA NOTICE
slides.description:
The FCRA requires notice when the adverse decision is based upon:

  1. Information contained in a consumer report
  2. If no consumer report is used, when a decision is based either wholly or partly on information obtained from a person other than a consumer reporting agency bearing upon the consumer's credit worthiness, credit standing, credit capacity, character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living.

slides.title: Make a Decision
slides.description:
• If the application is not complete, the creditor needs to either notify the applicant of its incompleteness and request the missing information or deny the application because it is incomplete. Under the later scenario an Adverse Action Notice needs to be sent.
  • Counter offers are slightly different in that they must be sent out within 90 days of the counteroffer given to the customer.
  • A creditor needs to make a decision on every application it receives. If an application is complete, the creditor needs to decide whether to approve it, deny it, or make a counteroffer.

slides.title: Information Required
slides.description:
• The name and contact information of the credit reporting agency, including: Address, Toll free Number and Web address.
  • If the credit decision was based in whole or in part on the information from a credit report, a statement that the reporting agency played no part in the decision and is unable to supply specific reasons why it denied credit to you.
  • That the customer has the right to a free credit report if requested within 60 days of receiving the notice.
  • That the customer has the right to question the accuracy and completeness of the content of their credit report.
  • If reasons for denial are not stated in the notice

slides.title: Form Notice
slides.description: Federal Regulations provide that a combined Adverse Action Notice containing requirements for both the FCRA and ECOA may be used. These form notices are found in Reg B, Appendix C. Use of Form Notices as set out in Reg B, provide a safe Harbor.

slides.title: EXAMPLE #1
slides.description:
Scenario:

The credit score is less than anything that has ever been accepted by the credit sources you do business with and the decision is made to not send the statement to anyone and the prospect is let go.

Response:

In this scenario you must send an adverse action notice.

slides.title: EXAMPLE #2
slides.description:
Scenario:

You spot deliver a car and submit the application to multiple lenders. No one accepts the terms as they were established on the retail installment contract. One did agree to extend the loan under modified terms and you renegotiate with the customer and he/she agrees to the new terms.

Response:

You do not need to send out an adverse action notice. However, if the customer does not agree to the new terms, and you take back the vehicle, you would have to send out a notice

slides.title: EXAMPLE #3
slides.description:
Scenario:

A credit statement is sent to multiple sources and it is rejected by all but one who has agreed to extend credit to the customer but under modified terms. The dealer does not agree to the terms and decides not to do the deal.

Response:

You must then issue and adverse action notice.

slides.title: CONCLUSION
slides.description:
The best way to look at adverse action notices is that:

  • Any time the dealer makes a decision to not send the credit statement to any lender notice is sent.
  • Any time the dealer decides not to accept the modified terms of a lender, send notice.
  • Any time the credit statement is completely rejected by all lenders, then an adverse action notice must be sent

questions.question: If the credit statement is taken over the phone(Five Liner) just to see if there is a chance that the applicant could get credit we do not have to issue an adverse action notice because there was no real expectation that the credit would be accepted.
We do not have to send an adverse action notice if:

answers.a: The terms that were acceptable to the lender were different than the original terms requested and you spotted the car but the customer would not accept the new terms and the deal was unwound.
answers.b: The customer submitted the statement through the 800 credit help line and it was sent around but was not acceptable to any lender but because it was through the bad credit 800 phone line there is no need to issue an adverse action notice.
answers.c: The customer submitted the statement and we ran the bureau and found a credit score of 350 and knowing there was no way we could get financing we informed the applicant that there was nothing we could do for them and they left but because we did not submit it to any lender there is no need to issue an adverse action notice.

questions.question: It is appropriate to send out adverse action letters:

answers.a: No later than 30 days after receiving the statement.
answers.b: Within 90 days of any counter offer given to an applicant where the new terms were not acceptable.
answers.c: Immediately upon the decision being made.

questions.question: The rule that governs the issuance of adverse action notices is the Truth In Lending Act or TILA.
